opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated questions in the whole "AI for science" conversation. Everyone focuses on the capabilities, whether an agent can write code, run experiments, and draft a paper, but the bottleneck at scale might be the social and incentive layer rather than the technical one.

Right now academic incentives are built around individual credit. You publish a paper, your name is on it, you get citations, and that turns into grants, positions, and tenure. That works reasonably well when a handful of humans do a project over six months. It starts to break when you have a swarm of agents generating thousands of hypotheses, running experiments in parallel, and building on each other's partial results, with humans steering or verifying along the way. Who gets credit? Is it the person who wrote the prompt, the person who built the agent scaffold, the people who curated the data, the reviewer who caught the subtle bug? Our current system has no good way to attribute that.

So I see a few things that need to shift.

First, we need to reward contributions more granularly. Not just the polished paper at the end, but the negative result, the reproducibility check, the dataset, the evaluation harness, the verified intermediate finding. In a distributed system, those small pieces are the infrastructure everything else stands on, and currently they're almost worthless on a CV. If you think about open source, there's at least some reputation economy around maintaining a widely used library. Science needs something similar, with provenance tracking so you can trace which contributions fed into which discoveries.

Second, verification has to become a first-class, rewarded activity. Agents can generate far more claims than humans can check. If review stays an unpaid, invisible favor, the system floods with plausible-looking but unverified output and trust collapses. So I think people, and probably also automated checkers, who do rigorous verification, replication, and red-teaming of results should get real credit. In a sense, the scarce resource shifts from generating ideas to validating them.

Third, we need to move away from novelty as the dominant currency. The pressure to show something new and flashy pushes people to hoard ideas and avoid sharing early. In a world with automated agents, sharing early and openly is what lets the system compound. If my half-finished idea gets picked up by an agent somewhere else and turned into a result, I want that to feel like a win for me rather than being scooped. That requires a cultural change and probably some technical mechanism for recording who seeded what.

And finally, there's the question of compute and access. If only a few labs can afford to run these large-scale agentic discovery loops, you don't really get distributed discovery, you get centralized discovery with a few names on top. So funding bodies and institutions should think about shared compute, open agent frameworks, and open archives of experiments, including failures, so the broader community can actually participate.

I'm optimistic, though. We've seen in machine learning that open benchmarks, open code, and preprints changed the culture pretty fast once the incentives lined up. I think something similar can happen here, but someone has to deliberately design it rather than hoping the old publish-or-perish model adapts by itself.

r001.rationale: The response says participation needs redesigned incentives: granular credit and rewards for contributions and verification, alongside funding and access mechanisms.

r002.rationale: The response mentions benchmarks and evaluation harnesses, but does not propose expanding leaderboards for numerically scored scientific work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions, and it's maybe less of a technical question than a sociological one. Right now the entire incentive structure of science is built around a very specific unit, which is the paper, and a very specific attribution model, which is the author list. And both of those things start to break down pretty quickly once you have agents in the loop.

Let me give a concrete example. When we worked on the AI Scientist, one of the things that became obvious very fast is that the system can generate a huge volume of hypotheses, experiments, and write-ups. Most of them are mediocre, some of them are wrong, and a small fraction are genuinely interesting. The bottleneck shifts entirely from generation to evaluation and curation. But our current incentive system rewards generation. You get credit for the paper you produced, not for the hundred ideas you correctly killed. So if you just plug agents into the existing system, you get a flood of low-signal output and you overwhelm peer review, which is already running on volunteer labor and goodwill.

So I think the first thing that has to change is that we need to start rewarding verification and reproduction as first-class scientific contributions. Historically that's been low-status work. Nobody gets tenure for replicating someone else's result. But in a world where agents can produce results cheaply, the scarce and valuable thing becomes trust. If I can trust that a result is real, that's worth a lot more than the result itself. And agents can actually help here too, because they can run replications at scale. But someone has to be incentivized to set that up and stand behind it.

The second thing is attribution. The author list is a terrible interface for this. What does it mean to have an agent as a co-author? I don't think that's quite the right frame. I'd rather think about it in terms of provenance. Every claim in a paper should have a traceable chain back to who or what produced it, what the inputs were, how it was checked. Something closer to a version control history than a byline. That way a human researcher who orchestrated a hundred agent runs and selected the right one gets appropriate credit for the judgment, and the system that did the mechanical work is acknowledged for what it actually did.

The third piece, and this is maybe the most radical one, is that I think we need to move away from the paper as the atomic unit entirely. Papers are these monolithic artifacts that bundle together an idea, an experiment, an interpretation, and a narrative. That bundling made sense when humans were the only producers. But distributed discovery works better when contributions are smaller and more composable. A hypothesis, an experimental result, a negative result, a dataset, an evaluation. If you can get credit for a well-documented negative result that saves ten other groups from wasting time, that changes behavior in a way that I think is very healthy.

And the last thing I'd say is about openness. For this kind of distributed system to work, agents and humans both need access to the same substrate. If results are locked behind paywalls or if the code never gets released, agents can't build on it and neither can humans at other institutions. So the incentive to be open has to go up. Funding agencies have some leverage here, and honestly I think the community has leverage too. We've already seen in machine learning how arXiv plus GitHub became a de facto publication system that moved much faster than journals. I think something analogous will happen here, but it has to be designed with a bit more care, because the failure mode of agents flooding an open commons with noise is very real.

So to summarize, reward verification, make attribution about provenance rather than bylines, shrink the unit of contribution, and push hard on openness. None of these are easy, and I don't think any single lab or company can do it alone. But I'm fairly optimistic, because the pressure is going to come whether we design for it or not. The agents are going to produce the output. The question is just whether we build the structures to make that output trustworthy and useful.

r001.rationale: The response says the incentive structure must change and proposes rewarding verification, reproduction, provenance-based credit, and openness, communicating mechanisms to sustain participation.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose expanding leaderboards for scientifically scored work.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to reward contributions that make the collective process work, even when they don’t produce a paper on their own. At the moment, the visible unit of credit is usually the publication. But if you build a useful environment, reproduce somebody’s result, or discover that a promising approach doesn’t work, that can save everyone else an enormous amount of effort. Those contributions need to count.

Once you bring automated agents into this, the problem becomes even more interesting. You can generate lots of hypotheses and experiments, but then the scarce resource becomes attention: which results should we trust, and which should we build on? If we reward sheer output, we’ll get sheer output. We need incentives for verification and for producing artifacts that other people—or other agents—can actually use.

I’d be interested in systems where credit follows that reuse. You contribute a method or an experimental result, somebody builds on it, and the provenance remains visible. But I wouldn’t assume there’s one metric that solves this, because whatever metric you choose will become a target.

So I’d start with smaller communities where contributions are traceable and quality is assessable. Can we make sharing an intermediate result more valuable than keeping it private until publication? If we can do that reliably, then we have a much better foundation for scaling distributed discovery.

r001.rationale: It discusses rewarding useful contributions and designing incentives, but does not clearly propose economic mechanisms or mechanism design for sustaining participation.

r002.rationale: It does not propose expanding leaderboards or scoring scientific work numerically.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to get better at rewarding contributions at a much finer granularity. Right now, the main unit of credit is a paper, and that bundles together a lot of different work: coming up with an idea, building infrastructure, running experiments, interpreting results. If you want humans and automated agents to collaborate at scale, you need some way of making those individual contributions visible and tracing how they helped produce a result.

But visibility alone isn't enough. If you reward the number of experiments or hypotheses someone generates, you'll get a lot of experiments and hypotheses, without necessarily learning much. You want to reward things that other people can actually build on: a reproducible result, a useful tool, or a negative result that rules out a promising-looking direction.

And I think there's a tension there, because the value of a contribution often only becomes clear much later. So I wouldn't expect one simple scoring mechanism to solve this. You probably need a combination of stable support for exploratory work and more direct rewards for contributions that prove useful. Agents make generating scientific output cheaper; the scarce resource becomes our ability to check it and decide what deserves attention. The incentive system has to support that part of the process as well.

r001.rationale: It calls for an incentive system combining stable support for exploratory work with direct rewards for useful contributions, addressing sustained participation in human–agent scientific discovery.

r002.rationale: It discusses making contributions visible and rewarding useful outputs, but does not propose leaderboards for numerically scored scientific work.
